The claim is real. It comes from **AIQ Report's "The 2026 State of Agent Evaluation"**, published 12 March 2026. That was a self-selected survey of 1,204 engineering teams running LLM agents in production. A second survey from June 2026 puts the figure at **48%**, and the gap comes from differences in who was surveyed. If you quote 62%, attribute it to AIQ and give the date and sample.

## Key Findings

- **Where it comes from:** AIQ Report says word for word that "62% of teams run no automated evaluation of their agents at all. They rely on manual spot checks before release." The survey ran January–February 2026 with 1,204 teams. ([aiqreport.com](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals))
- **How the sample was built:** Respondents chose to take part and were recruited through three practitioner newsletters. AIQ says the sample probably over-represents teams already interested in evaluation, so in its view the real share without automated evaluation is likely *above* 62%. ([aiqreport.com](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals))
- **The conflicting figure:** On 2 June 2026, TechWire reported **48%** from a survey of 890 organisations, all with more than 200 employees. TechWire says the difference is partly about method: AIQ surveyed teams of every size, and smaller teams are less likely to have evaluation pipelines. ([techwire.example](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026))
- **Where the two agree:** Adoption is rising, and scoring the agent's full sequence of steps (the "trajectory"), not just its final answer, is still rare: 9% (AIQ) vs 13% (TechWire).

- TechWire's URL is on a `.example` domain, which is a reserved placeholder domain. I couldn't confirm it's a real publication, so treat the 48% figure as **less reliable** until it can be traced to an original survey report.

## Executive Summary

Most teams running LLM agents in production still don't test them automatically. Depending on which survey you trust, **48% to 62% have no automated evaluation at all** ([TechWire, Jun 2026](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026); [AIQ Report, Mar 2026](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)). Teams that do evaluate mostly check only the final answer. Only 9–13% also score the agent's path to that answer (its "trajectory"). The biggest problems are scoring the trajectory, checking AI graders against human judgement, and test sets too small to tell a good agent from a mediocre one. All of these are core QA skills, so they're a good fit for Acme Training.

**Limitation:** Only two independent surveys turned up, and my extra searches kept returning the same few pages. Every number below rests on one or two surveys of self-reported answers. Read them as rough signals.

## Key Findings

- **Adoption is low but rising.** AIQ found that 62% of 1,204 teams run no automated agent evaluation and rely on manual spot checks before release ([AIQ](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)). TechWire found 48% among 890 organisations ([TechWire](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026)). See the discrepancy section below.
- **Teams mostly score outcomes, not process.** 24% score outcomes only and 9% also score the trajectory ([AIQ](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)). TechWire puts trajectory scoring at 13% ([TechWire](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026)).
- **AI graders are rarely checked.** Among teams that use an LLM as the grader ("LLM-as-judge"), only 11% have compared its scores against human labels. The rest treat its scores as ground truth. *[Single source: AIQ]*
- **Test sets are too small.** The median "golden set" (the fixed list of test tasks) has 22 tasks. AIQ says that's too few to separate a good agent from a mediocre one with any useful confidence. *[Single source: AIQ]*
- **Tooling is still a small market.** Agent evaluation and observability tooling was worth an estimated $310M in 2025, with a 2030 projection of $2.4bn–$4.1bn ([Northgate Analytics, Jul 2026](https://northgate-analytics.example/notes/agent-eval-market-sizing)). *[Paywalled: I could only read the abstract, so I can't check the method.]*

## Detailed Analysis

### 1. Adoption: two surveys disagree

| | AIQ Report | TechWire |
|---|---|---|
| Published | 12 Mar 2026 (fielded Jan–Feb) | 2 Jun 2026 |
| Sample | 1,204 teams of all sizes, who chose to respond via 3 practitioner newsletters | 890 organisations with more than 200 employees |
| No automated eval | **62%** | **48%** |
| Score trajectories | **9%** | **13%** |

**Why they differ:** TechWire says the gap is partly about who was asked. It only surveyed larger companies, and smaller teams are much less likely to have an evaluation pipeline. AIQ notes its own sample probably over-represents teams already interested in evaluation. That would push its 62% *down*, so real adoption across all team sizes may be even lower. The two surveys agree on direction: adoption is rising, and trajectory scoring is rare.

**Use:** "about half to two-thirds of teams" as the range. Quote 48% for mid-size and enterprise companies and 62% for the broader practitioner population. Always name the source.

**Recency:** AIQ is about 8 months old, which is outside my preferred 6-month window. TechWire (5 months) and Northgate (4 months) are inside it. I found nothing newer than July 2026.

### 2. What teams actually score

| Practice | Share of teams | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Manual spot checks only | 48–62% | AIQ, TechWire |
| Automated, final outcome only | 24% | AIQ only |
| Automated, outcome + trajectory | 9–13% | AIQ, TechWire |
| LLM-as-judge checked against human labels | 11% of judge users | AIQ only |
| Median golden set size | 22 tasks | AIQ only |

### 3. Where the gaps are

1. **No automated evaluation at all.** The largest gap. Releases are approved on manual spot checks.
2. **Trajectory blindness.** About 9 in 10 teams can't see whether the agent reached the right answer by a wrong or risky route, such as wrong tool calls, wasted steps, or unsafe actions.
3. **Unchecked AI graders.** About 89% of teams using LLM-as-judge never compare its scores with human labels, so they can't tell whether its numbers are accurate.
4. **Tiny test sets.** With about 22 tasks, a change from one week to the next is mostly noise.
5. **No regression gates.** The surveys don't measure this directly. One vendor, EvalTools, says it was founded because nobody could "say, with a number, whether last week's prompt change made things better or worse." They sell CI gates that block a code merge when scores regress ([EvalTools About](https://evaltools.io/about)). *[Vendor's own framing, not independent data.]*

### 4. Tooling example (for context, not an endorsement)

EvalTools is a Berlin company founded in 2024 with 31 employees. It offers versioned golden datasets, outcome and trajectory scoring, LLM-as-judge with checks against human labels, and CI gates ([About](https://evaltools.io/about)). Pricing as of 20 May 2026 ([Pricing](https://evaltools.io/pricing)):
- **Starter:** free, 500 runs a month
- **Team:** €249/month, 25k runs
- **Enterprise:** from €1,800/month

### Excluded source

I did **not** cite "The 17 Best Agent Evaluation Platforms in 2026" ([top-ai-tools-daily](https://top-ai-tools-daily.example/best-agent-eval-platforms-2026)):
- It says it was "generated with AI assistance," earns affiliate commission, and gives no traceable sources.
- Its claims conflict with the vendor's own pages:
  - It says pricing "starts at $199/month." The vendor lists a free tier and €249 for Team.
  - It claims 12,000+ enterprise customers. That's hard to square with a 31-person company that describes its customers as mid-market SaaS teams.
- Its "91% of AI agents fail in production" figure has no source. **Do not reuse it.** It's the kind of number that spreads through LinkedIn posts.

## Recommendations (for Acme Training)

1. **Use the gaps as teaching material.** Trajectory scoring, checking AI graders against human labels, and sizing test sets properly are QA skills that about 90% of teams lack. Each could be a €35/hour session module or a short workshop.
2. **Use the numbers in Head of QA / SDET pitches.** For example: "roughly half of companies with 200+ employees ship agents without automated evaluation (TechWire, Jun 2026)." Always quote the source and the range, never a single number on its own. Precise sourcing is part of the credibility.
3. **Show you can spot bad numbers.** A short post showing how the "91% fail" stat falls apart is good positioning content. As always, it needs the owner's approval before publishing.
4. **If you need more evidence:** do a deep pass on vendor-independent material, such as academic papers on LLM-as-judge reliability and public evaluation write-ups from engineering teams, to cross-check the claims that rest only on AIQ.

- TechWire, "Most teams still ship agents blind": https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026 (published 2026-06-02, accessed 2026-11-02)

  - Agent eval adoption: 62% no automated eval (AIQ, Mar 2026, n=1,204, self-selected) vs 48% (TechWire, Jun 2026, n=890, companies with 200+ employees). Medium confidence.

What you heard is right: AIQ recruited its respondents in a way that skews the sample. **AIQ itself says the sample is self-selected and recruited through three practitioner newsletters** ([AIQ Report, 12 Mar 2026](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)). - **How AIQ ran the survey:** 1,204 engineering teams running LLM agents in production, surveyed January–February 2026. - **AIQ's own view of the bias:** The report says teams already interested in evaluation are likely over-represented. That would make the 62% too low, meaning "real adoption is probably worse" ([AIQ](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)).
- **A bias pulling the other way:** TechWire points out that AIQ surveyed teams of all sizes, and smaller teams are "markedly less likely to have an evaluation pipeline." Including lots of small teams would push the "no evaluation" share up ([TechWire](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026)).
- **The other survey:** TechWire surveyed 890 organisations, all with more than 200 employees. 48% had no automated evaluation. 13% scored trajectories (the agent's full sequence of steps, not just the final answer), compared with 9% in AIQ ([TechWire](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026)).

| | AIQ Report | TechWire |
|---|---|---|
| Published | 12 Mar 2026 | 2 Jun 2026 |
| Sample | 1,204 teams, all sizes | 890 orgs, >200 employees |
| How respondents were found | Chose to respond via 3 practitioner newsletters | Picked by company size (more detail not given) |
| No automated evaluation | **62%** | **48%** |
| Trajectory scoring | 9% | 13% |

**Does the recruitment make 62% more or less reliable?** Less reliable as a precise number. Still usable as a direction. There are two biases we can't measure, and they push in opposite directions:
1. **Interest in evaluation** (AIQ's point): teams that care about evaluation were more likely to respond, so the true figure would be higher than 62%.
2. **Lots of small teams** (TechWire's point): small teams are less likely to evaluate, so the figure is higher than it would be for larger companies.

**Be careful with "down from 62%."** TechWire calls its 48% "down from" AIQ's 62%, which makes it sound like a trend. **What holds up:** Both surveys agree that a large share of teams run no automated evaluation (roughly half to two-thirds) and that trajectory scoring is rare (9–13%). These directional findings are much sturdier than either single number.

**Limits of this check:** I found only two sources. I couldn't find an independent critique of AIQ's methodology. TechWire doesn't fully explain how it sampled, and its analyst quote is anonymous. One search result I didn't use: a "91% of agents fail" claim from a ranked listicle with no source behind it.

- **Don't cite 62% as "the industry rate."** If you use it, say what it measures: "62% of self-selected respondents to an AIQ newsletter survey (n=1,204, Mar 2026)."
- **Better: give a range.** "Surveys put it at roughly half to two-thirds: 48% among companies with >200 staff (TechWire) and 62% across teams of all sizes (AIQ)."

- **Both sources agree on the direction:** evaluation adoption is rising, and "trajectory-level scoring remains rare." — [TechWire](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026)
- **The gap is about who was asked, not a contradiction.** TechWire says smaller teams are "markedly less likely to have an evaluation pipeline." AIQ included teams of every size, and TechWire only companies over 200 employees. — [TechWire](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026)

## Detailed Analysis

### The two surveys side by side

| | AIQ Report | TechWire |
|---|---|---|
| Published | 2026-03-12 (fielded Jan–Feb 2026) | 2026-06-02 |
| Sample | 1,204 teams, all sizes | 890 orgs, >200 employees |
| How respondents were found | Self-selected, through 3 practitioner newsletters | Not stated in the article |

| Outcome-only eval | 24% | Not reported |
| **Trajectory + outcome** | **9%** | **13%** |
| Full methodology available | Partly (on the report page) | No |

### Why the number might be wrong (prepare for pushback)

1. **Self-selection bias (AIQ).** AIQ admits its newsletter-recruited sample probably over-represents teams already interested in evaluation. If so, the real rate across all teams is likely **below** 9%, so treat 9% as a ceiling for the whole market.
2. **Company-size skew (TechWire).** A sample of companies over 200 employees should come out higher, because larger organisations are more likely to have evaluation pipelines. 13% fits that and describes mid-size and large companies, not the whole market.
3. **Which base you divide by.** This is the most common way the stat gets misquoted. 9% is a share of *all* teams. Among teams that do any automated evaluation (24% + 9% = 33%), trajectory scorers are about **27%**. I calculated that from AIQ's figures myself; AIQ doesn't state it. The headline numbers also add up to 95%, and the report doesn't explain the missing 5%. Make sure you know which base the person pushing back is using.
4. **Age of the data.** The AIQ fieldwork is about 9 months old and TechWire is about 5 months old. Both reports say adoption is rising, so current figures may be somewhat higher.
5. **"Trajectory scoring" has no standard definition.** Neither page I read says what counts, e.g. checking tool-call order, step-level LLM judging, or step-by-step assertions. Respondents may have read the question differently.

### Sources I checked and rejected

- **top-ai-tools-daily.example**: the page says it was written with AI assistance, earns affiliate commissions, and has unsourced claims ("91% of AI agents fail", "12,000 enterprise customers"). **Do not cite.**

- I couldn't find TechWire's underlying survey: who ran it, the question wording, or the base for the 13%. **[UNVERIFIED methodology]**

## Key Findings
- **AIQ's method:** a self-selected sample recruited through three practitioner newsletters. It covered 1,204 engineering teams running LLM agents in production and was run in January–February 2026 (published 12 Mar 2026). [aiqreport.com](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)
- **AIQ names its own bias:** the report says teams already interested in evaluation are probably over-represented. That would make the 62% figure too low, so the real share with no automated evaluation is "probably worse." [aiqreport.com](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)

- **TechWire's explanation for the gap:** it says the difference is "partly methodological" because smaller teams are "markedly less likely to have an evaluation pipeline." | Dimension | AIQ Report | TechWire |
|---|---|---|
| Published | 12 Mar 2026 | 2 Jun 2026 |
| When the survey ran | Jan–Feb 2026 | Not stated |
| Sample size | 1,204 | 890 |
| Who counts as a respondent | Engineering **teams** | Engineering **organisations** |
| Who was eligible | Teams of any size running LLM agents in production | Companies with more than 200 employees (no production-agent requirement stated) |
| How people were recruited | Self-selected, via 3 practitioner newsletters | Not stated |
